chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from Ibrahim ibn Maymun, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a town belonging to some people of the Ahl al-Zimma (people of the covenant). I do not know if its origin (ownership) was theirs or not, other than that it was in their hands and upon them was the land tax (kharaj). So the Sultan (ruling authority) exceeded upon them, and they sought me out, so they gave me their land and their town on the condition that I would suffice them against the Sultan with whatever amount (of tax), whether little or much. So the excess would be for me after that, a remainder after what the Sultan takes whatever he takes. He (peace be upon him) said: There is no problem with that; for you is whatever was from the excess.

key_terms.أَهْلِ الذِّمَّةِ: People of the covenant (non-Muslims under Muslim rule)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on keeping the surplus tax after paying the Sultan's demand for leased Ahl al-Zimma land?
ai.summary: This hadith illustrates the practical application of *kharaj* (land tax) in early Islamic governance, where a Muslim could assume the fiscal responsibility for non-Muslim subjects (*Ahl al-Zimma*) through a lease or guarantee (*kafala*) arrangement. Imam al-Sadiq’s validation confirms that the lessee retains any surplus after fulfilling the state's tax obligation, highlighting the flexibility of property rights and tax collection mechanisms in Shia jurisprudence. This ruling underscores the distinction between personal poll tax (*jizya*) and land tax, allowing for private contractual arrangements in managing communal fiscal duties.
